pointers.sentence: So a decorator whose wrapper uses the request cannot be written above a handler method as it stands, and `method_decorator` exists to adapt it (`django/utils/decorators.py:method_decorator`).

On `dispatch` it does so where `dispatch` would run, inside the function `as_view` returned, after `View.setup` (`django/utils/decorators.py:_multi_decorate`, `django/views/generic/base.py:View.as_view`).

A partial takes them: those `functools.wraps` sets on it there, the method's name among them, and any the decorator sets on what it is given (`django/utils/decorators.py:_multi_decorate`).

So `_multi_decorate` also applies each decorator once, when the class is made, to a stand-in, a function that does nothing, and copies whatever attributes the stand-in comes back with onto the replacement (`django/utils/decorators.py:_update_method_wrapper`).

It copies what decorators left on `dispatch` onto the function it returns, so a mark on `dispatch` reaches the URLconf and a mark on `post` stays on `post`, where no middleware looks (`django/views/generic/base.py:View.as_view`).

Given a list of decorators, `_multi_decorate` applies them from the last to the first, so that the first in the list is outermost, as if they had been written one above another in that order (`django/utils/decorators.py:_multi_decorate`).

Only `login_not_required` leaves a mark, `"login_required"` set false, and `as_view` copies it onto the function it returns (`django/contrib/auth/views.py:LoginView`, `django/contrib/auth/decorators.py:login_not_required`).
